data.title: Wall Street Breakfast: What Moved Markets This Week
data.description:
Listen on the go! A daily podcast of Wall Street Breakfast will be available by 8:00 a.m. on Seeking Alpha, iTunes, Spotify.

Up for a challenge? Test your knowledge on the biggest events in the investing world over the past week. Take the latest Seeking Alpha News Quiz and see how you stack up against the competition.

Wall Street closed the week mixed as a sharp spike in volatility reflected fresh tech struggles, while investors continued to digest hotter-than-expected CPI data and the latest bank earnings.

CPI inflation heated up in September. On a year-over-year basis, the Consumer Price Index rose 3.7%, matching the consensus forecast and accelerating from a 3.4% gain in August.The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged roughly 30% on Friday afternoon to trade above 21, reaching a more than four-month high as tech stocks continued to struggle.

Big banks kicked off Q3 earnings season as traders digested results from Goldman Sachs (GS), JPMorgan (JPM), Citigroup (C), Wells Fargo (WFC), and other major lenders.

For the week, the blue-chip Dow (DJI) added +0.67%, the benchmark S&P (SP500) lost -1.95%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) plunged -4.48%. Read a preview of next week's major events in Seeking Alpha's Catalyst Watch.

'Wrecking ball'

The UN is sounding the alarm on this year's El Niño, with the agency's emergency relief chief Tom Fletcher describing it as "a wrecking ball" that will bring extreme heat, droughts and floods. While El Niño is a normal climate pattern, it's expected to be unprecedented this year. This year appears similar to the 1997-98 event that caused an estimated $5.7T in global income losses. data.title: Weyerhaeuser: Profound Mispricing
data.description:
In a previous article we showed that at private timberland values, Weyerhaeuser’s (WY) 9.74 million owned acres are worth $26.2B which demonstrates a substantial gap between asset value and WY’s valuation.

Since then, new data has come out showing that timberland values have continued to rise while WY’s stock price has continued to fall. It has created a historically wide disconnect between public and private pricing with WY trading at 50% of net asset value.

We shall begin by showing the disparate movement of underlying asset value with WY’s stock price and follow with a look at what a 50% discount to NAV means in this asset class with WY’s capital structure.

Value up – price down

Timberland value is best measured by actual transactions that take place. FRC and Fastmarkets compiled transaction data to show average transaction price per acre over time.

Source

Transaction values generally rose from about $1,800 per acre in 2018 to just over $2,500 per acre in 2025.

That is roughly what one would expect in an inflationary period. Timberland values have continued to rise in 2026. NCREIF reports timberland appreciation of 3.28% year-over-year in 1Q26 and another 0.61% in 2Q26

In 2026 timberland values have been rising at a pace slower than inflation. This is likely due to rising interest rates which mathematically pull down the value of long duration assets.

Nonetheless, timberland values are up in 2026. Contrast that with WY’s stock price down 20%.

WY was already steeply discounted to asset value in 2025. I thought it was a great deal buying it at 66% of NAV.

So far, I have been quite wrong on the stock price. However, I have mostly been right on the fundamentals. Key earnings metrics are showing excellent current year and future growth.

Below are the consensus estimates of Wall Street analysts covering WY:

2026 is coming in substantially higher than 2025 in FFO, AFFO, revenue and EBITDA. Growth is forecast to accelerate into 2028 with FFO rising 83% from 2025 levels. 2028 EBITDA is roughly 70% higher.

Good things are happening at the company. They have innovative products like TimberStrand and operate mills and timberlands with superior efficiency to competitors.

Mill curtailments across Canada and smaller operators in the U.S. are materially reducing competition which has kept lumber prices stable despite the slowdown in housing driven by high mortgage rates.

7.5% mortgage rates are a tough operating environment for the entire housing industry. It seems the market has painted the industry with a broad bearish brush, selling nearly all participants in unison.

The selloff has been agnostic to valuation and agnostic to individual company fundamentals. In my opinion, WY selling down an additional 20% in 2026 from an already highly discounted level has taken it to an absurd discount.

Profound mispricing

WY’s consensus NAV is $37.16

At today’s $18.84, it is trading at 50.7% of NAV.

REITs historically trade mostly between 90% and 105% of NAV. Occasionally, something slips through the cracks or has underlying problems that can result in substantially deeper discounting.

We have observed 50% of NAV magnitude of discounting primarily in the following types of companies:

  • Microcaps
  • Extremely high leverage (80%+ capital structure is debt/preferred)
  • Misaligned management (RMR companies, Ashford companies)
  • Troubled asset class (office and malls)

WY stands out because it distinctly doesn’t have the problems above.

  • Market share leader as the largest timberland owner in the U.S.
  • Large cap
  • Investment grade balance sheet (BBB)
  • Respected management that outperforms on key operating metrics

Perhaps the market is viewing and pricing timberland as a troubled asset class. I think there is a big difference between a cyclical downturn and structural damage.

Lumber is absolutely in a cyclical downturn, but I haven’t heard any legitimate talk of it being a permanently impaired industry. Eventually, houses will have to be built as there is already a housing shortage.

50% of NAV in a historical context

In order for the discount at which WY trades to make sense there would have to be legitimate risk that timberland values could drop enough to close the gap in that direction.

Timber/lumber is a highly stable industry that has been around for centuries and through dozens of business cycles. I want to examine what a 50% discount means in a stable industry, so we shall look at some of the most severe downturns in history to see what happened to asset values.

Housing bubble – home prices declined 18.9% peak to trough.

Prices peaked at an indexed level of 380 in 2007 and dropped to a 308 trough in 2012. That is an 18.9% decline from peak to trough.

The USDA documents the largest agricultural land value decline of the century at 37% and it happened during the Great Depression which hit simultaneously with the physical damage of the Dust Bowl.

“Agricultural land values saw the largest percentage declines of the century in the early 1930s, the beginning of the Great Depression. Agricultural land values dropped 37 percent over a period of 3 years and remained between $30 and $33 per acre throughout the 1930s.”

In both cases, asset values rebounded sharply and sustainably after the trough.

I posit that what WY is dealing with is a run-of-the-mill housing recession brought on by a sharp rise in mortgage rates.

It is nowhere near the severity of the housing bubble popping in the Great Financial Crisis or the Dust Bowl amidst the Great Depression.

Even in such severe cases, the 50% discount at which WY trades would be enough to more than offset the drawdowns in asset value. Note that timberland values have actually risen so far in 2026. They may not decline at all in this cycle as land tends to be a great asset class in a higher than target inflation environment.

When the housing cycle eventually turns, WY will be the largest operator in an environment where competition has been substantially shrunk due to curtailments. It takes years for those competing mills to come back online, and WY did not have to shut down operations due to higher operating margins. WY has been strongly EBITDA positive through the entire downturn, positioning it to capture significant market share.

Risks to WY

I think there is a decent chance WY misses estimates in 3Q26 due to the timing of changes in interest rates. Through the first half of 2026, interest rates and mortgage rates were stable.

Suddenly, in 3Q26, mortgage rates shot up to 7.5%

This likely had an acute depressive impact on housing activity.

WY and analysts were forecasting a somewhat weak environment, but I don’t think guidance was anticipating the sharp rise in rates. Lumber prices held up, but volume suffered.

In terms of overall valuation, I don’t think a weak 3Q26 is all that impactful. However, a miss could cause further damage to WY’s stock price in the near term.

The bottom line

WY is trading at profoundly cheap levels that don’t make sense for a company of its caliber. While it is difficult to predict the cadence of recovery in stock price, I think buying at these levels will eventually be rewarded with strong returns as the stock price eventually moves toward NAV.
